title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Recap: DFM & tf-idf

Corpus → tokens → DFM → tf-idf weighting
Rows = docs, columns = terms, cells = (weighted) frequency

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Supervised vs. unsupervised learning

Supervised: labeled data, learn a mapping inputs → outputs (classification, regression) — our focus today
Unsupervised: no labels, discover structure (clustering, topic modeling) — see the Day 1 notes if you want to explore this on your own
Target feature: gender (female/male); predictor: the biography text
Split into train (80%) / test (20%) sets — watch for class imbalance when splitting

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Dictionaries

Predefined word lists mapped to categories (e.g. pronouns → gender)
Classify by counting dictionary-word occurrences per document


dict_gender <- dictionary(list(
  female = c("she","her","hers","herself"),
  male   = c("he","him","his","himself")
))
dfm_pron <- dfm_lookup(dfm_all, dict_gender)

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Naive Bayes Classification

Probabilistic classifier based on Bayes’ Theorem
“Naive”: assumes features are conditionally independent given the class
Widely used for high-dimensional data like text


nb_train <- textmodel_nb(x = dfm_train, y = y, prior = "docfreq")
predict(nb_train, newdata = dfm_test, type = "class")

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Model evaluation
\[Accuracy = \frac{\text{Correct}}{\text{Total}} \quad
Precision = \frac{TP}{FP+TP} \quad
Recall = \frac{TP}{FN+TP}\]
\[F_1 = 2 \times \frac{Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall}\]

Class imbalance → the model may just always predict the majority class

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Task

Why do we track precision/recall separately instead of just accuracy?
Why might the true negative rate be zero on an imbalanced set?
Bonus: build a STEM vs. non-STEM prize classifier

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
What are word embeddings?

“You shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth, 1957)
Represent each word as a dense vector; similar meaning → nearby vectors
Pre-trained on huge corpora: Word2Vec, GloVe, fastText
Window size = how many words of context count around a target word

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
How are they trained?

Model predicts a masked word from context (“the ___ chased the ball”)
Compares its guess to the real word, updates weights via gradient descent
Words that co-occur often end up with nearby vectors

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Loading embeddings & nearest neighbors

library(data.table)
emb <- fread("path/to/embeddings.txt", header = FALSE, quote = "")
words <- emb[[1]]
glove <- as.matrix(emb[, -1, with = FALSE])
rownames(glove) <- words

glove["dog", ]   # look up a word's vector


library(text2vec)
sims <- sim2(glove, matrix(glove["woman", ], nrow = 1))
names(sort(sims[, 1], decreasing = TRUE))[1:7]

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Visualization

Reduce embedding dimensions (PCA) down to 2 for plotting
Closer points ≈ closer meaning


Z <- prcomp(glove[c("einstein","curie","nobel","peace"), ])$x[, 1:2]

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
What are Large Language Models?

Deep learning models trained on vast text corpora to model language
Foundation models → pre-trained, general-purpose
LLMs → foundation models specialized for language tasks
Fine-tuning vs. prompting (zero-shot / few-shot)
Prefer prompting first — fine-tuning is costly and data-hungry

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Why are LLMs so powerful?

All LLMs are transformer models
Attention — weighs the importance of each word when predicting the next one
Captures long-range dependencies better than RNNs/LSTMs

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Feedforward neural networks

Information flows one direction: input → hidden layer(s) → output
No cycles; every node connects to every node in the next layer, each connection weighted


Feedforward neural network

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Transformer Models

Stack of encoders + decoders
Encoder: self-attention + feedforward layers → rich input representation
Decoder: generates output using that representation, also via self-attention
Trained via next-word prediction & masked-word prediction


Transformer model

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Running local LLMs with Ollama

Ollama runs open LLMs (e.g. Llama) locally
No cloud dependency, full control over the model


library(rollama)
list_models()
ping_ollama()

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
System vs. user prompts

System prompt — assigns a role & constraints (“You are a research assistant…”)
User prompt — the task-specific instruction + content


question <- "Task: classify whether this biography summary
  describes a female or male Nobel laureate."
query(paste(question, df$extract[1]), model = "llama3.1")

title: Day Two (Half Day)
text:
Task

Zero-shot classify a handful of biography summaries by gender using rollama
Compare the LLM’s predictions to the Naive Bayes classifier from earlier today — where do they agree/disagree, and why?

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text: Welcome to this R Studio tutorial. It’s intended to support the in-person walkthrough and is a bit more detailed, with exercises included along the way.

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
Download R and R Studio
To use R Studio, first download R, then R Studio — in that order. R is the programming language; R Studio is the interface. Use posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop for both, or get R directly from CRAN. Make sure the R version matches your operating system and, on a Mac, your processor. After downloading, the installer should start automatically.

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
R Studio interface & Markdown
On the right side of the screen is the console — the window where commands are executed. Executed code and any error messages appear here, but the commands themselves are not saved. On the upper left is the Environment tab — your workspace, listing all relevant objects, variables, and data sets currently in use. Below that there are several more tabs; the Help tab is particularly useful, giving access to function documentation.

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
What are packages?
Packages are collections of commands, which must be loaded into R Studio before they can be used — the same way you have to be taught something before you can apply it.
Installing a package (name in quotation marks, since it’s a string):

# install.packages("pacman")

Packages only need to be installed once. Before an already-installed package can be used, it needs to be loaded — this time without quotation marks:

library(pacman)

Loading packages one by one every session is tedious. The pacman package solves this: p_load() installs and loads packages in one call.

pacman::p_load("haven", "tidyverse", "rmarkdown")

haven lets us import files saved in Stata format (.dta).
Datasets also need to be loaded into R Studio, from a file saved on your computer (or a URL). Every file has a path — its address — which we need to specify in order to read it in.

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
Creating objects
R is an object-based language: we store information in objects, which are containers for values. This could be a single variable (e.g. “age”) or a whole dataset (rows = observations/cases, columns = variables).
Below, we create an object called fruit (a vector) using the assignment arrow <-. c() (“combine”) lists the values it should contain.

fruit <- c("apple", "pear", "grapes")

fruit[2]

price <- c(2, 1, 4)

R is case-sensitive — "h" and "H" are different characters. It helps to write everything in lowercase to avoid this source of error.

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
Creating a dataset
Beyond single vectors, we can build small datasets — e.g. combining the fruit and price vectors with cbind():

basket <- cbind(fruit, price)
basket <- as.data.frame(basket)
View(basket)

With this mini dataset we can already run some calculations:

mean(price)     # arithmetic mean
median(price)   # median
min(price)      # smallest value in the column
max(price)      # largest value in the column
sum(price)      # sum of the column
summary(price)  # all of the above, at once


Exercise

Create a dataset from any two variables. Three cases is plenty. One variable should hold numeric values, the other characters.

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
Importing a dataset
Working directory — the path where your dataset lives. Once set, you only need to specify the file name, not its full path. Set it with setwd(); check the current one with getwd(). An incorrect working directory is a common reason a dataset fails to load.
Finding a file’s path — on a Mac, click the file in Finder, then right-click (or Control-click) and choose “Copy … as Pathname.” On Windows, right-click the file → Properties → “Location” gives the folder, and you still need to append the file name and extension. Windows paths use double backslashes (\\) instead of a single slash (/).






Tip



The example below reads a CSV file. There are other common formats, e.g. Stata’s .dta, readable in R via the haven package’s read_dta(). Swap in whichever dataset and format you’re using for this session’s exercises.



df <- read.csv("path/to/your/dataset.csv")

Check the Environment pane (top right) to confirm the dataset loaded — it’ll show the number of observations and variables.

View(df)

If variable names aren’t self-explanatory, check the dataset’s codebook for more detailed descriptions. Always review a dataset before using it.

Overview of variables

ncol(df)  # number of columns
nrow(df)  # number of rows


names(df)  # variable names

Access a specific variable with $:

summary(df$age)

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
Creating tables
table() builds a frequency table; prop.table() converts it to proportions. To interpret these you need to know how the variables are coded.

gender_distribution <- table(df$female)
gender_distribution

proptable <- prop.table(gender_distribution)
round(proptable, digits = 2)


urban_distribution <- table(df$urban)
urban_distribution

proptable <- prop.table(urban_distribution)
round(proptable, digits = 2)

Cross-tabulation — same table() function, just add a second variable after the comma:

tab_2 <- table(df$female, df$urban)  # gender x urban/rural
tab_2

The result isn’t very readable without knowing the coding — here, female: 0 = male, 1 = female; urban: 0 = rural, 1 = urban. Add labels with dimnames():

dimnames(tab_2) <- list(gender = c("male", "female"), residence = c("rural", "urban"))
tab_2


proptable <- prop.table(tab_2)
round(proptable, digits = 2)

# proptable_cols <- prop.table(tab_2, margin = 2)  # column-wise proportions


Exercises
Importing data

Load the Titanic dataset.

Describing data

What object class does the variable pclass (passenger class) have?
How many women and men were on the Titanic?

Descriptive results

What was the average ticket price (median and mean; variable fare)?
What was the average age of the Titanic passengers?
How many children did Mr. Anders Johan Andersson have on board?

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
Visualizations
hist() gives a quick overview of a variable’s distribution:

hist(df$age)

For more flexible graphics, use ggplot2 — see this cheat sheet. A boxplot:

# Preprocessing before plotting
df$female <- as.factor(df$female)
df <- df[!is.na(df$female), ]
df <- df[!is.na(df$age), ]

df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = female, y = age, group = female)) +
  geom_boxplot()


Exercises

Visualize the distribution of a variable.
Visualize a variable a different way.

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
Piping
Data outside of seminars is rarely clean — it needs preparation. For data wrangling, chain multiple commands together with piping. Assign to a new object with <-, specify the dataset, then chain tidyverse commands with %>% (Mac: Shift+Cmd+M, Windows: Ctrl+Shift+M). Pressing Enter after a pipe automatically indents the next line — no need to repeat the dataset name, and the last line doesn’t need a trailing pipe.

df_clean <- df %>%
  select(female, happy, trust, income) %>%  # pick specific columns
  filter(female == 1) %>%                    # pick specific rows
  rename(gender = "female")                  # rename a variable

# na.omit(df_clean$income)  # drop missing values


What’s the difference between = and ==?
Two equals signs (==) make a comparison and return TRUE/FALSE. A single equals sign is an assignment operator.


Exercises
Data preprocessing

Rename the variable sex to gender.
Create a sub-dataset with at least three variables, containing only passengers who survived the Titanic.
Remove all missing values from the dataset.

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
If-else statements
Most data wrangling can be done with tidyverse functions, but sometimes it’s easier to think in if-then conditions.
We want a new variable that’s "low" when income is ≤ 5, and "high" otherwise:

df_clean$income_category <- ifelse(df_clean$income <= 5, "low", "high")
View(df_clean)

title: Setup: First Steps with R Studio
text:
Getting help with error messages
Error messages are completely normal in R — the cause isn’t always obvious, and it helps to look for support:

The Help tab (bottom right) has documentation for specific functions and commands.
RPubs and Stack Overflow are great community resources — code can often be copied and adapted.
An LLM (e.g. ChatGPT) can help debug faulty code or explain what a snippet does, so you build a solid understanding rather than just copy-pasting.

title: Day 1 Notes
text: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is an interdisciplinary field between computer science and linguistics, which ultimately aims to quantitatively represent text in such a form that computers can understand it. The methods developed within NLP are used in a variety of different fields and applications, such as sociology, political science, and various private companies. Due to the growing availability of digital trace data, NLP has become a transformative subfield that affects most people’s daily lives through the latest advances in machine learning.

title: Day 1 Notes
section: Let’s talk a bit about Wikipedia
text:
Let’s talk a bit about Wikipedia
Wikipedia is a free online encyclopedia, created and edited by volunteers around the world and hosted by the Wikimedia Foundation since 2001. It is one of the largest and most popular general reference works on the internet, with millions of articles in multiple languages. Wikipedia is written collaboratively by largely anonymous volunteers who write without pay. Anyone with internet access can write and make changes to Wikipedia articles, except in limited cases where editing is restricted to prevent disruption or vandalism.
Wikipedia is a reflection of our contemporary knowledge production — it crucially shapes what people know and how they remember the past. Wikipedia is influencing media content, scientific research, foundational for generative AI, and ordinary citizens’ real-life decisions. Journalistic work has additionally shown that political groups proactively seek to edit Wikipedia in their favor, such as politicians or far-right actors (. Previous research has shown that number editors on Wikipedia are limited and predominantly male, reflecting persisting patterns of gender inequality in other aspects of society.

title: Day 1 Notes
text:
Web Scraping
The current advances in machine learning, combined with the growing amount of digital data, have led to a new interest in NLP. Web scraping is the process where we “scrape” data from the web, which is then used to train a model. Compared to traditional data collection methods, web scraping allows us to gather far more data in a much shorter time.
We can either scrape data from a website (static) or from an Application Programming Interface (dynamic). The latter is often more efficient, as it allows us to access data directly from the source without having to parse HTML. rvest is a package that helps you scrape data from web pages statically. We’re scraping the award table on this Wikipedia page.

# Install and import packages
# install.package("pacman")
library(pacman)
pacman::p_load("rvest", "tidyverse")

# Define the URL of the page we want to scrape
url <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates")

# Extract the table from the page
nobel_table <- url %>%
  html_node("table") %>%   # selects the first table on the page
  html_table()              # converts the HTML table to a data frame


API
Scraping data through the Wikipedia web API is relatively easy. An API is a piece of software that allows two pieces of software to talk to each other, in most cases through an HTTP request — similar to the request your browser sends when it asks a server for a page’s HTML.
The process is roughly always the same:

You connect to the URL of your API, e.g. en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php
You send an HTTP GET request to the API with specific parameters — this tells the API what you want.
You retrieve a response, usually in JSON.


library(httr2)

get_last_revision <- function(page_title, continue_parameter = NULL,
                               user_agent = "Polmem_ucl") {
  baseurl <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php"

  params <- list(
    action  = "query",
    format  = "json",
    titles  = as.character(page_title),
    prop    = "revisions",
    rvprop  = "ids|timestamp|user|userid|comment|size|content",
    rvslots = "main",
    rvlimit = 1,       # just the latest
    rvdir   = "older"  # newest first; single item is current revision
  )

  if (!is.null(continue_parameter)) params$rvcontinue <- continue_parameter

  resp <- request(baseurl) %>%
    req_user_agent(user_agent) %>%
    req_url_query(!!!params) %>%
    req_perform()

  json <- resp_body_json(resp)

  pages <- json$query$pages
  if (is.null(pages) || !length(pages)) return(data.frame())

  pg <- pages[[1]]
  if (is.null(pg$revisions) || !length(pg$revisions)) return(data.frame())

  rv <- pg$revisions[[1]]
  slots <- rv$slots$main

  data.frame(
    page_title    = pg$title %||% NA_character_,
    page_id       = as.character(pg$pageid %||% NA),
    revid         = as.character(rv$revid %||% NA),
    parentid      = as.character(rv$parentid %||% NA),
    user          = as.character(rv$user %||% NA_character_),
    userid        = as.character(rv$userid %||% NA),
    timestamp     = as.character(rv$timestamp %||% NA_character_),
    size          = as.character(rv$size %||% NA),
    comment       = as.character(rv$comment %||% NA_character_),
    contentmodel  = slots$contentmodel %||% NA_character_,
    contentformat = slots$contentformat %||% NA_character_,
    content       = slots[["*"]] %||% NA_character_,
    check.names = FALSE,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

# Applying the function
page_content_revision <- get_last_revision("List of Nobel laureates")



Using Wrappers
For most relatively accessible APIs, someone has built a wrapper. There exist two main wrappers for Wikipedia in R: WikipediR and wikkitidy. We use the WikipediR package, which lets us send requests to the Wikipedia API in just a few lines of code. We only need to specify the language, the project, and the page name. Unfortunately, WikipediR does not parse the HTML for us, so we use the XML package to parse it and extract the table.

library(WikipediR)
library(XML)

# WikipediR wrapper
page_content_nobel <- WikipediR::page_content(
  language = "en", project = "wikipedia",
  page_name = "List of Nobel laureates", clean_response = TRUE
)

# Parsing the html
parsed_html <- htmlParse(page_content_nobel, asText = TRUE)
first_table <- readHTMLTable(parsed_html, which = 1, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
colnames(first_table) <- first_table[1, ]
first_table <- first_table[-1, ]



Task

Scrape the biographies of the female and male Nobel laureates from Wikipedia. You can do this dynamically or statically — if dynamically, use the WikipediR or wikkitidy package.
Wikipedia helps us here via its category structure: scrape all pages and their content under Category: Lists of Nobel laureates.

One approach: use pages_in_category() from WikipediR to retrieve all pages within the “Women Nobel laureates” category. There isn’t a similar category for men, so pivot the nobel_table scraped earlier, filter out the names, and merge.

# Retrieving all pages in the category (but not content yet)
all_pages_category_women <- WikipediR::pages_in_category(
  "en", "wikipedia", categories = "Women Nobel laureates",
  clean_response = TRUE
)
all_pages_category_women <- all_pages_category_women[-c(1, 2), ]

nobel_table <- nobel_table %>%
  slice(-n()) %>%
  pivot_longer(-Year, names_to = "category", values_to = "laureates") %>%
  rename(title = laureates)

women <- left_join(all_pages_category_women, nobel_table, by = "title") %>%
  select(title, category, Year) %>%
  mutate(gender = "female")

men <- nobel_table %>%
  filter(!title %in% women$title) %>%
  mutate(gender = "male")

all_winners <- bind_rows(women, men)



Show solution
# preprocess the scraped data to get a clean list of names
names_tbl <- all_winners %>%
  filter(!is.na(title), nzchar(title), tolower(str_trim(title)) != "none") %>% # delete all empty cells
  # drop “no award” rows that are just dashes (any kind)
  filter(!str_detect(title, "^[[:space:]]*[—–-]+[[:space:]]*$")) %>%
  # some cells have multiple winners separated by semicolons
  separate_rows(title, sep = "\\s*;\\s*") %>%
  # strip bracketed citation markers like [a], [13]
  mutate(title = str_remove_all(title, "\\[(?:\\d+|[A-Za-z])\\]")) %>%
  mutate(title = str_squish(title)) %>%
  filter(!title %in% c("None", "List of women Nobel laureates", "Cancelled due to World War II")) %>%
  filter(nzchar(title))

# unique vector of names
all_names <- names_tbl %>%
  distinct(title) %>%
  arrange(title) %>%
  pull(title)

summaries_pages <- data.frame()

for (title in all_names) {
  
  summary_page <- tryCatch(wikkitidy::get_page_summary(language = "en", title = title),
    error = function(e) NULL)
  
  if (!is.null(summary_page)) {
    summaries_pages <- bind_rows(summaries_pages, summary_page)
  }
}

title: Day 1 Notes
text:
Data Preparation
A pre-scraped data set is provided, containing all summaries of the biographies of all award winners, with columns:

pageid — unique identifier for each Wikipedia page
title — the Wikipedia page title (the laureate’s name)
extract — the summary of the biography
revision — unique identifier for the specific page revision
gender — whether the awarded individual was female or male

⬇ Download wikipedia_nobel_biographies_summaries_clean.parquet (226 KB)

library(arrow)

clean_text_data <- read_parquet("../data/wikipedia_nobel_biographies_summaries_clean.parquet")
glimpse(clean_text_data)

clean_text_data <- clean_text_data %>%
  drop_na(title)

# Gender distribution
proptable <- prop.table(table(clean_text_data$gender))
round(proptable, digits = 2)

Looking at the gender distribution reveals how imbalanced Nobel prizes are with respect to gender — only about 4.6% of all prizes were awarded to women. Let’s find out how these women are depicted on Wikipedia.

Optional Task
⬇ Download wikipedia_nobel_biographies_summaries_clean_extended.parquet (229 KB)

Read the wikipedia_nobel_biographies_summaries_clean_extended.parquet data set and store it in a new object.
Drop NA values in the title variable.
Select a subset of columns, but keep the gender column.
Filter out only female instances.



Show solution

wiki_summaries_ex <- wiki_summaries_ex %>%
  drop_na(title) %>%

title: Day 1 Notes
text:
Text Preprocessing
Text preprocessing transforms raw text data into a clean, structured format suitable for analysis. Scraping your own data is often painful — the goal of preprocessing is to enhance the quality of the text by removing noise, inconsistencies, and irrelevant information.
We first create a corpus — our set of documents with their corresponding text (e.g. different Wikipedia articles). A corpus consists of documents, which consist of sentences, which consist of terms.
Common preprocessing techniques:

Tokenization — breaking text into smaller units (words, phrases, or sentences).
Lowercasing — ensures uniformity and reduces complexity.
Removing punctuation and special characters — these usually don’t contribute to meaning.
Removing stop words — common words (“and”, “the”, “is”) that don’t carry much meaning.
Stemming and lemmatization — reduce words to their base/root form.

We use the quanteda package for text preprocessing.

library(quanteda)

# Create corpus
corpus <- corpus(clean_text_data, text_field = "extract", docnames = "pageid")

# Tokenization
tokens <- corpus %>%
  tokens(remove_punct = TRUE,
         remove_symbols = TRUE) %>%
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en"), padding = FALSE) %>%
  tokens_tolower() %>%
  tokens_compound(pattern = clean_text_data$title, concatenator = "_", case_insensitive = FALSE) %>%
  tokens_compound(pattern = "nobel prize", concatenator = "_", case_insensitive = FALSE) %>%
  tokens_wordstem()

title: Day 1 Notes
text:
The Document-Feature Matrix (DFM)
A Document-Feature Matrix (DFM), or Document-Term-Matrix (DTM), is a structured representation of text data that captures the frequency or presence of words (features) across a collection of documents. Rows represent documents, columns represent unique terms, and each cell holds the frequency of a term in a document. With many words and few documents the matrix gets very sparse — watch out for the Curse of Dimensionality!
A DFM is a crucial step in NLP: it transforms unstructured text into a structured format that statistical and machine learning techniques can work with. It holds a few key assumptions (“bag of words”):

The words in a document convey meaning.
Word order does not matter.
Word combinations do not matter (i.e. negation).
Grammar does not matter.
Words are the only relevant features (not punctuation, not syllables, etc).




Document-Feature Matrix


Most words do not appear in every document, so the matrix easily gets sparse. We can trim the DFM to remove very rare and very frequent words. Counting raw term prevalence implicitly assumes all words are equally important, which is often not the case — so we apply tf-idf weighting. It reflects how important a word is to a document in a collection: importance increases with how often a word appears in the document, offset by how common the word is across the whole corpus.
\[TF = \frac{\text{count of term } t \text{ in document}}{\text{total terms in document}}\]
\[TF\text{-}IDF = TF \times \ln\!\left(\frac{\text{total documents}}{\text{documents containing } t}\right)\]
Worked example

d1: “red car fast”
d2: “blue car slow car”

DFM (counts):
    blue car fast red slow
d1     0   1    1   1    0
d2     1   2    0   0    1
Term Frequency (TF = count / doc length):

d1: blue=0, car=0.333, fast=0.333, red=0.333, slow=0
d2: blue=0.25, car=0.5, fast=0, red=0, slow=0.25

Document Frequency (DF, N = 2 docs): blue=1, car=2, fast=1, red=1, slow=1
Inverse Document Frequency (IDF = ln(N/df)): blue=0.693, car=0, fast=0.693, red=0.693, slow=0.693
TF-IDF (tf × idf):
     blue   car  fast    red  slow
d1   0.000  0.000  0.231  0.231  0.000
d2   0.173  0.000  0.000  0.000  0.173

Optional Task: calculate a small DFM by hand

d1: “The quick brown fox”
d2: “The lazy dog”

DFM (counts):
    the quick brown fox lazy dog
d1    1     1     1   1    0   0
d2    1     0     0   0    1   1
TF (d1 has 4 tokens, d2 has 3 tokens):
    the  quick brown  fox lazy  dog
d1  0.25 0.25  0.25  0.25 0.00 0.00
d2  0.33 0.00  0.00  0.00 0.33 0.33
DF: the=2, quick=1, brown=1, fox=1, lazy=1, dog=1. IDF = ln(2/df): the=0.000, quick=0.693, brown=0.693, fox=0.693, lazy=0.693, dog=0.693.
TF-IDF:
    the    quick  brown   fox   lazy   dog
d1  0.000  0.173  0.173  0.173  0.000  0.000
d2  0.000  0.000  0.000  0.000  0.231  0.231


Calculating the DFM with quanteda
We take our tokens object and call dfm() on it. We usually want to trim the DFM (removing very rare and very frequent words), then apply tf-idf weighting to reduce sparsity. min_termfreq = 0.8 with termfreq_type = "quantile" keeps only the top 20% most frequent terms across the corpus (the bottom 80% of rare words get cut).

# Create a document-feature matrix (DFM)
dfm <- dfm(tokens) %>%
  dfm_trim(min_termfreq = 0.8, termfreq_type = "quantile")

# tf-idf weighting
dfm_tfidf_mat <- dfm_tfidf(dfm)



Task

Build a corpus for female and male award winners separately.
Preprocess the text (tokenization, lowercasing, removing punctuation and special characters, removing stop words, stemming/lemmatization).
Look at what preprocessing options quanteda offers.
Create a DFM for both corpora.



Show solution
clean_text_female <- clean_text_data %>% filter(gender == "female")
clean_text_male   <- clean_text_data %>% filter(gender == "male")

corpus_female <- corpus(clean_text_female, text_field = "extract", docnames = "pageid")
corpus_male   <- corpus(clean_text_male, text_field = "extract", docnames = "pageid")

tokens_female <- corpus_female %>%
  tokens(remove_punct = TRUE, remove_symbols = TRUE) %>%
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en"), padding = FALSE) %>%
  tokens_tolower() %>%
  tokens_wordstem()

tokens_male <- corpus_male %>%
  tokens(remove_punct = TRUE, remove_symbols = TRUE) %>%
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en"), padding = FALSE) %>%
  tokens_tolower() %>%
  tokens_wordstem()

dfm_female <- dfm(tokens_female)
dfm_male   <- dfm(tokens_male)

title: Day 1 Notes
section: Text Analysis Workflow for Bag-of-Words Models
text:
Text Analysis Workflow for Bag-of-Words Models
The general workflow typically involves:

Data collection — gather text data from websites, social media, or documents.
Text parsing — break text into tokens, stem words, remove stop words.
Text filtering — weight your terms.
Text modeling — apply statistical or machine learning models (topic modeling, sentiment analysis, classification).




Text Analysis Workflow


There are no general rules for preprocessing decisions — it always depends on your data and research question. Try out different preprocessing steps and see how they affect your results.

title: Day 2 Notes (Half Day)
text:
This page picks up where Day 1 left off (clean_text_data, etc.) — datasets can be downloaded from the Data Preparation section there.
In supervised learning we have labeled data — we want to learn a model that predicts a target feature. For example, given a biography summary, predict whether it’s of a female or male award winner: the gender column is our target feature, and the text is our predictor.
To build a model that generalizes well, we split data into training and test sets. The training set trains the model; the test set checks how well it does on unseen data. One pitfall: with an imbalanced data set, make sure the target feature’s distribution is similar across both sets (see Model evaluation below).

library(arrow)
library(quanteda)
library(quanteda.textmodels)

clean_text_data <- read_parquet("../data/wikipedia_nobel_biographies_summaries_clean_extended.parquet")

clean_text_data <- clean_text_data %>%
  filter(pageid != 7152417)

set.seed(123)
clean_text_data$train <- sample(x = c(TRUE, FALSE),
                                 size = nrow(clean_text_data),
                                 replace = TRUE,
                                 prob = c(.8, .2))

corpus <- corpus(clean_text_data, text_field = "extract", docnames = "pageid")

dfm <- corpus %>%
  tokens() %>%
  dfm() %>%
  dfm_remove(stopwords("en"))

dfm_train <- dfm_subset(dfm, train)
dfm_test  <- dfm_subset(dfm, !train)

dim(dfm_train)  # 808 documents, 8239 tokens
dim(dfm_test)   # 200 documents, 8239 tokens

title: Day 2 Notes (Half Day)
text:
Dictionaries
Dictionaries are a classic tool in text analysis: a predefined list of words associated with specific categories or sentiments. Each dictionary word is assigned to one or more categories, allowing classification of text based on the presence of these words.

set.seed(123)

clean_text_data$train <- sample(c(TRUE, FALSE),
                                 size = nrow(clean_text_data),
                                 replace = TRUE,
                                 prob = c(.8, .2))

corp <- corpus(clean_text_data, text_field = "extract", docnames = "pageid")
toks <- tokens(corp, remove_punct = TRUE) %>% tokens_tolower()
dfm_all <- dfm(toks)

# which words could we add?
dict_gender <- dictionary(list(
  female = c("she", "her", "hers", "herself"),
  male   = c("he", "him", "his", "himself")
))

dfm_pron_all   <- dfm_lookup(dfm_all, dict_gender)
dfm_pron_train <- dfm_subset(dfm_pron_all, train)
dfm_pron_test  <- dfm_subset(dfm_pron_all, !train)

pred_test <- ifelse(dfm_pron_test[, "female"] >  dfm_pron_test[, "male"], "female",
              ifelse(dfm_pron_test[, "female"] <  dfm_pron_test[, "male"], "male", NA))
pred_test <- factor(pred_test, levels = c("female", "male"))

y_test <- factor(docvars(dfm_pron_test, "gender"), levels = levels(pred_test))

caret::confusionMatrix(pred_test, y_test)


Naive Bayes Classification
Naive Bayes (NB) is a simple yet effective probabilistic classifier based on Bayes’ Theorem. It predicts the most likely class by comparing the probabilities of each class given the observed features. The “naive” assumption is that features are conditionally independent given the class, which simplifies computation. NB is widely used in high-dimensional tasks like text classification.
In plain terms: given some conditions, it answers “which outcome is most probable?” For example, given that the weather is rainy and the temperature is 6°C, Naive Bayes can estimate the probability someone will (or won’t) play golf, and classify accordingly.

y <- factor(docvars(dfm_train, "gender"))
nb_train <- textmodel_nb(x = dfm_train, y = y, prior = "docfreq")

class_test <- predict(nb_train, newdata = dfm_test, type = "class")
docvars(dfm_test, "pred_nb") <- class_test

confusion_test <- table(
  predicted = docvars(dfm_test, "pred_nb"),
  truth     = docvars(dfm_test, "gender")
)
confusion_test

The model mostly predicts “male” when the winner actually was male — unsurprising, since male award winners are highly over-represented in the data. Predicting “male” is always a good guess when the target is this skewed — a class imbalance, a well-known ML problem. There are several techniques to tackle it, such as upsampling the minority class.


Model evaluation
A model can make two kinds of mistakes: falsely classifying instances as female when they were male (false positives), and classifying instances as male when they were actually female (false negatives). We have several indicators to assess model performance:
\[Accuracy = \frac{\text{Correctly Classified}}{\text{Total Classifications}}\]
\[Precision = \frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{False Positives} + \text{True Positives}}\]
\[Recall = \frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{False Negatives} + \text{True Positives}}\]
Recall is also called Sensitivity or the True Positive Rate.
\[F_1 = 2 \times \frac{Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall}\]


Task

Why do we have so many different measurements? Why are we interested in the rates of true positives and true negatives separately?


library(caret)
confusion_test_statistics <- confusionMatrix(confusion_test, positive = "female")
confusion_test_statistics


Why is our true negative rate zero?



Task

Can we build a predictor for STEM vs. non-STEM prizes?


clean_text_data$stem <- ifelse(
  clean_text_data$category %in% c("Chemistry", "Physiologyor Medicine", "Medicine", "Physics"),
  "STEM", "non-STEM"
)

corp <- corpus(clean_text_data, text_field = "extract", docnames = "pageid")
toks <- tokens(corp, remove_punct = TRUE) %>% tokens_tolower()
dfm_all <- dfm(toks)

dfm_train <- dfm_subset(dfm_all, train)
dfm_test  <- dfm_subset(dfm_all, !train)

y <- factor(docvars(dfm_train, "stem"))
nb_train <- textmodel_nb(x = dfm_train, y = y, prior = "docfreq")

class_test <- predict(nb_train, newdata = dfm_test, type = "class")
docvars(dfm_test, "pred_nb") <- class_test

confusion_test <- table(
  predicted = docvars(dfm_test, "pred_nb"),
  truth     = docvars(dfm_test, "stem")
)
confusion_test

confusion_test_statistics <- confusionMatrix(confusion_test, positive = "STEM")
confusion_test_statistics

title: Day 2 Notes (Half Day)
text:
Word Embeddings
“The meaning of words is defined by the company they keep” (Firth, 1957). We represent meaning using a vector for each word, constructed so that words similar in meaning are also close together in vector space. The goal is a dense vector per word, similar to the vectors of words that appear in similar contexts. These representations are called word embeddings, because we “embed” words into a low-dimensional space (low compared to the vocabulary size).
Word embeddings are pre-trained on large corpora, e.g. Wikipedia. The most common approaches are Word2Vec, the GloVe project, and fastText — all require substantial computational power and data to train.
Windows — if a word’s meaning is defined by the company it keeps, we can define a window size: how many words before and after the target word count as context.
Imagine a model tasked with predicting a masked word — “the ___ chased the ball”, “the ___ is a pet”. It starts by randomly guessing the embedding for the hidden word. During training the model sees the actual word, compares it to its own prediction, and updates its weights via gradient descent to do better next time. To reduce mistakes, it generates vectors that are closer together for words that frequently appear together in its n-dimensional space.

Gradient descent, in short: compute the slope of the loss with respect to each parameter, and move a tiny step downhill.


df <- arrow::read_parquet("../data/wikipedia_nobel_biographies_summaries_clean.parquet") %>%
  drop_na()


library(data.table)

# path to your embeddings file
path <- "path/to/your/glove_or_dolma_embeddings.txt"

# Read GloVe-style file (no header line, unlike fastText)
emb <- fread(path, header = FALSE, quote = "", encoding = "UTF-8")

# Split into words + vectors
words <- emb[[1]]
glove <- as.matrix(emb[, -1, with = FALSE])
rownames(glove) <- words

# Example: look up vector for "dog"
glove["dog", ]

dim(glove)  # e.g. 1,200,001 terms x 300 dimensions


library(text2vec)

similarities <- function(target_word, n) {
  # Extract embedding of target word
  target_vector <- glove[which(rownames(glove) %in% target_word), ]

  # Calculate cosine similarity between target word and other words
  target_sim <- sim2(glove, matrix(target_vector, nrow = 1))

  # Report nearest neighbours of target word
  names(sort(target_sim[, 1], decreasing = TRUE))[1:n]
}

similarities("woman", n = 7)
similarities("men", n = 7)


library(text2vec)
library(quanteda)

# Construct corpus
corp <- corpus(df, text_field = "extract")

# Create vocab list based on dfm
vocab <- featnames(
  dfm(tokens(corp, remove_punct = TRUE) %>%
        tokens_tolower() %>%
        tokens_remove(stopwords("en")))
)

# Create function that selects the nearest neighbors
nearest_from_summaries <- function(glove, query, top_n = 20, vocab = NULL) {
  rn   <- rownames(glove)
  cand <- if (is.null(vocab)) glove else glove[rn %in% vocab, , drop = FALSE]

  # expand wildcards (case-insensitive) and collect matches
  to_rx <- function(q) paste0("^", gsub("\\*", ".*", tolower(q)), "$")
  matches <- unique(unlist(lapply(query, function(q)
    grep(to_rx(q), rn, ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)
  )))

  q_vec <- colMeans(glove[matches, , drop = FALSE])

  sims <- text2vec::sim2(cand, matrix(q_vec, nrow = 1),
                          method = "cosine", norm = "l2")[, 1]

  sims <- sims[setdiff(names(sims), matches)]
  sort(sims, decreasing = TRUE)[1:top_n]
}


# "female concept" neighbours (woman, women, female*)
nn_female <- nearest_from_summaries(glove,
  query = c("woman*", "women", "female*"),
  top_n = 20, vocab = vocab
)

# "male concept" neighbours (man, men, male*)
nn_male <- nearest_from_summaries(glove,
  query = c("man", "men", "male*"),
  top_n = 20, vocab = vocab
)

nn_female[1:20]
nn_male[1:20]

title: Day 2 Notes (Half Day)
text:
Visualization
We can also plot word embeddings, reducing their dimensions to two. The closer terms are to one another, the closer they are in meaning.

library(ggplot2)

show_map <- function(words) {
  M <- glove[intersect(words, rownames(glove)), , drop = FALSE]
  Z <- prcomp(M, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)$x[, 1:2]

  df <- data.frame(Z, word = rownames(Z))
  ggplot(df, aes(PC1, PC2, label = word)) +
    geom_point() + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 3)
}

show_map(c("einstein", "curie", "planck", "nobel", "physicist", "chemist",
           "literature", "ernaux", "peace", "literatur", "peac", "united"))

title: Day 2 Notes (Half Day)
text:
Large Language Models (LLMs)

What are Large Language Models?
Large Language Models (LLMs) are advanced AI models designed to understand, generate, and manipulate human language. They’re built using deep learning, particularly neural networks, and trained on vast amounts of text data to learn language’s statistical patterns and structures. A useful distinction: foundation models are pre-trained on a large corpus and can be fine-tuned for specific tasks; LLMs are a subset of foundation models specifically designed for NLP tasks.
Fine-tuning — take a pre-trained model and specialize it for a downstream task, by training on a smaller, task-specific dataset while keeping the pre-trained weights as a starting point. This adapts the model to a task’s specific nuances without training from scratch.
Prompting — instead of fine-tuning, provide specific prompts or instructions to guide the model’s behavior. More flexible and adaptable, without extensive retraining.
Two flavors of prompting:

Zero-shot learning — the model gets a task with no prior examples, relying solely on its pre-existing knowledge.
Few-shot learning — the model gets a small number of examples or demonstrations to help it understand the task’s context and requirements.

It’s usually best to start with prompting, and only fine-tune if prompting doesn’t work well enough — fine-tuning has high computational and labor costs and needs large amounts of labeled data.


Why are LLMs so powerful?
LLMs capture the complexities and nuances of human language, enabling a wide range of tasks with high accuracy: generating coherent, contextually relevant text, answering questions, translating, summarizing, and conversing. All LLMs are a form of transformer model. Transformers contain an attention mechanism that weighs the importance of different words in a sentence when making predictions — this captures long-range dependencies and context far more effectively than earlier models like RNNs or LSTMs, which is why LLMs are so transformational for the field.
What are feedforward neural networks?



Feedforward Neural Network Architecture


A feedforward neural network is an artificial neural network where connections between nodes don’t form a cycle — information flows in one direction, from the input layer through one or more hidden layers to the output layer. Each node in a layer connects to every node in the next layer, and each connection has a weight determining the strength of that connection.
See also: StatQuest — Feedforward Neural Networks.


Transformer Models



Transformer Model


A transformer model contains a stack of encoders and decoders. The encoder processes the input text through multiple layers of self-attention and feedforward networks to build a rich representation of the input. The decoder uses this representation to generate the output text, again through self-attention and feedforward layers. The attention mechanism lets the model focus on different parts of the input when generating each output word, capturing context and relationships effectively. Transformer models learn to understand language through next-word/sentence prediction and masking particular words.

title: Day 2 Notes (Half Day)
text:
Running Local LLMs with Ollama
Llama is an LLM developed by Meta and, unlike many competitors, is open source. It’s not as large as GPT-3 or GPT-4, but still powerful and usable for a variety of tasks. Ollama is a platform for running and managing LLMs on your local machine, with an easy-to-use interface for developers and researchers who want to leverage LLMs without extensive infrastructure or cloud services.

library(rollama)

# available models you have installed locally
list_models()

# pull_model("mistral:7B")  # download a model

ping_ollama()  # check if the Ollama server is reachable

System and user prompts are core components of prompt engineering. A system prompt gives the model foundational instructions — assigning a role (“You are a research assistant”) and constraints (ethical guidelines, style, behavior). System prompts are typically consistent across sessions. A user prompt contains task-specific instructions (“Classify these sentences into categories”), possibly with extra context or examples.
We’ll try zero-shot learning first: get some text, construct the prompt, and send it to the model.

# We can simply talk to the model
rollama::query("What is the capital of New York", model = "llama3.1")

# Construct the query: a system message assigns a role, then the
# user prompt supplies the task-specific text.
df$zero <- NA_character_

for (i in 1:2) {
  question <- "Task: You're a research assistant that helps to analyze texts. Your aim is to classify whether the summary of a biography describes a female or a male Nobel prize winner."
  text <- df$extract[i]
  question <- paste(question, text)
  result <- query(question, model = "llama3.1")
  print(result)
  df$zero[i] <- result[[1]]$message$content
}







Tip



That’s a lot of ground for half a day. If you’re tight on time in the room, the first candidates to trim are the word embeddings code walkthrough (keep the concept, skip live-coding the GloVe lookup) and the Ollama zero-shot loop (demo it live once rather than having everyone run it).

title: Day One
text:
Static vs. dynamic scraping

Static: scrape the rendered HTML of a page (e.g. rvest)
Dynamic: query an API directly (usually more efficient — no HTML parsing needed)


library(pacman); pacman::p_load("rvest", "tidyverse")

url <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates")
nobel_table <- url %>% html_node("table") %>% html_table()

title: Day One
text:
The Wikipedia API

Connect to the API URL, e.g. en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php
Send an HTTP GET request with parameters
Retrieve a response, usually JSON

title: Day One
text:
The Document-Feature Matrix (DFM)

Rows = documents, columns = terms, cells = frequency
Bag-of-words assumptions: word order & grammar don’t matter, only presence/frequency
Gets sparse fast → trim rare/frequent terms


DFM example

title: Day One
text:
tf-idf weighting
\[TF\text{-}IDF = TF \times \ln\!\left(\frac{N}{\text{docs containing } t}\right)\]

Raw counts assume every word is equally important — usually false
tf-idf up-weights words that are frequent in a document but rare across the corpus
dfm_trim() + dfm_tfidf() in quanteda

title: Day One
text:
Task: hand-calculate a DFM

d1: “The quick brown fox” / d2: “The lazy dog”
Compute counts → TF → DF → IDF → TF-IDF by hand
Then verify with dfm() + dfm_tfidf() in quanteda
